segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Again he went into a synagogue, and a man was there who had a withered hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were watching him closely to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they could accuse him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to the man with the withered hand,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Get up and stand in the middle.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save a life or to kill?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they stayed silent.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Looking around at them with anger, deeply grieved at the hardness of their hearts, he said to the man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Stretch out your hand.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisees went out and at once began plotting with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great multitude from Galilee followed; and from Judea

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and from Jerusalem and from Idumea and beyond the Jordan and around Tyre and Sidon a great multitude, hearing all that he was doing, came to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He told his disciples to have a small boat stand ready for him because of the crowd, so that they would not crush him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he had healed many, so that all who had afflictions were falling upon him to touch him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the unclean spirits, whenever they saw him, would fall down before him and cry out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are the Son of God!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he sternly warned them not to make him known.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went up the mountain and called to him those he himself wanted, and they came to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He appointed twelve, so that they might be with him and so that he might send them out to proclaim

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to have authority to drive out the demons.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he appointed the Twelve: to Simon he gave the name Peter;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to them he gave the name Boanerges, which means Sons of Thunder);

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Cananaean,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and Judas Iscariot, who also handed him over.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat bread.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When his family heard of it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He is out of his mind.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He has Beelzebul,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “By the ruler of the demons he drives out the demons.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he called them to him and spoke to them in parables:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How can Satan drive out Satan?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand but is at an end.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But no one can enter the strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man; and then he will plunder his house.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, everything will be forgiven the sons of men, their sins and whatever blasphemies they utter;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For they had been saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He has an unclean spirit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent word to him, calling him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, your mother and your brothers are outside looking for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Who are my mother and my brothers?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And looking around at those seated in a circle about him, he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Here are my mother and my brothers!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For whoever does the will of God, that person is my brother and sister and mother.”

notes.note: The Herodians are known only from the Gospels. The name suggests supporters or dependants of the Herodian dynasty, here most likely of Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee. Their exact identity is uncertain; an alliance between them and the Pharisees would have struck a contemporary reader as unusual.
This is the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake. Mark calls it a sea, following Semitic usage in which one word covers both lakes and seas; Luke calls it a lake.

notes.traditional: He appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles)
notes.note: Some early and important manuscripts add “whom he also named apostles” after “twelve.” The SBLGNT omits the words, judging them likely to have been carried over from Luke 6:13; other critical editions print them in brackets. The repeated clause “he appointed the Twelve” at the start of verse 16 is likewise absent from many manuscripts.

notes.traditional: Simon the Cananaean; Simon the Canaanite (KJV)
notes.note: The epithet does not mean “Canaanite” or “from Cana.” It transliterates an Aramaic word meaning “zealous one,” which Luke 6:15 gives in Greek as “the Zealot.” Whether it marks Simon as a militant nationalist or simply as a man of religious zeal is disputed.

The verb means to hand over or deliver up, and Mark uses the same word for John’s arrest (1:14) and for Jesus being handed over to the authorities and to Pilate. Greek had a distinct word for betrayal, which Luke 6:16 uses of Judas. Most translations render “betrayed” here, which fits the context, but that hides the thread Mark runs through his narrative with this one verb.
The Greek phrase can mean either “into a house” or “home.” The second is chosen here, on the assumption that the house in Capernaum mentioned at 2:1 is meant, but the first is equally possible.

The Greek is literally “those from beside him,” an expression used in the period for a person’s associates, household or relatives. Most interpreters take it as his family, since his mother and brothers arrive in verse 31; the KJV has “his friends.” It is also possible to read “for people were saying” rather than making the family the speakers.

Beelzebul is a name for the ruler of the demons, whom Jesus’ reply equates with Satan. Its derivation is debated; it is probably connected with a title of the Canaanite god Baal and with the Baal-zebub of 2 Kings 1. To “have” Beelzebul means to be possessed by him, as verse 30 makes clear.
This is a Semitic idiom meaning simply human beings. It is plural and general, and is not the title “Son of Man” that Jesus uses of himself.

Later manuscripts read “eternal judgment,” which lies behind the KJV’s “eternal damnation.” The earliest witnesses have “sin,” the harder reading, which scribes probably softened. In the Greek, “eternal” echoes the preceding “never,” which is literally “not into the age.”

notes.traditional: your mother and your brothers [and your sisters]
notes.note: Some manuscripts add “and your sisters” here. The SBLGNT omits the words; other editions print them in brackets. They may have been added in view of “sister” in verse 35, or dropped to match verses 31 and 33–34.

candidates.reason: Used of Judas, the authorities, Pilate and God across the Gospels and Paul; rendering it “betray” in some places and “hand over” in others hides a deliberate verbal thread.
Translations vary between “scribes,” “teachers of the law” and “legal experts,” and “scribe” may suggest a mere copyist to modern readers.
The Greek covers slander and abusive speech against people as well as God, so a policy is needed on when to use “blaspheme” and when “slander” or “revile.”
Jesus’ distinctive “Amen I say to you” formula recurs dozens of times, and translators differ between “truly,” “amen,” “verily” and “I assure you.”
Recurs in legal disputes across the Gospels and in Paul, where “lawful” and “permitted” are both common and should not alternate at random.
